summary.title: CUPID: for joyful coding
summary.one_liner: Dan North's CUPID framework describes five properties (Composable, Unix philosophy, Predictable, Idiomatic, Domain-based) that make code pleasant to work with, as an alternative to SOLID principles.
takeaways: Code quality can be assessed through five properties: Composable, Unix philosophy, Predictable, Idiomatic, Domain-based.
Properties are a direction of travel toward a centre, unlike rules, which are pass/fail compliance checks.
Unix philosophy (do one thing well, from the outside in) is distinct from the Single Responsibility Principle (one reason to change, from the inside out).
Predictable code is deterministic, observable, and behaves as expected; it generalizes testability.
Idiomatic code follows the conventions of its language and team, reducing cognitive load for future readers.
summary.summary: Dan North argues that SOLID principles are less useful today and proposes CUPID, five properties of software that make it joyful to work with. He explains why properties are preferable to principles, and the criteria a useful property should meet: practical, human, and layered. Each CUPID property is then discussed with heuristics, examples from Unix, Python, Go, and trading systems, and counterpoints such as trade-offs and the difference between SRP and single purpose. The article ends by introducing domain-based design, with the rest of the discussion about domain-based structure promised in the page text.
